content: Hyperkalaemia is a frequent electrolyte imbalance that occurs in patients with chronic kidney disease (CKD) due to impaired renal potassium excretion. Potassium binders, such as sodium polystyrene sulfonate and calcium polystyrene sulfonate, are commonly used to manage this condition. However, these older agents are associated with gastrointestinal side effects, including constipation, which can limit their tolerability. Newer potassium binders, such as patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate, have been developed and may cause fewer gastrointestinal side effects. Despite this, the safety profile of these newer agents remains inadequately studied, and evidence on their impact on clinically significant outcomes, such as cardiac complications or mortality, is limited. Given the increasing availability of treatment options, it is essential to evaluate the effectiveness and tolerability of all potassium binders in patients with CKD to guide clinical practice and policy decisions. The objective of this review was to assess the benefits and harms of potassium binders in treating chronic hyperkalaemia in adults and children with CKD. A systematic search was conducted in the Cochrane Kidney and Transplant Register of Studies up to March 10, 2020, using relevant search terms. The studies included in the register were identified through searches of CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, conference proceedings, the International Clinical Trials Register (ICTRP) Search Portal, and ClinicalTrials.gov. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomised controlled trials (quasi-RCTs) evaluating potassium binders in adults and children with CKD were included. Two independent reviewers assessed the risk of bias and extracted data from the studies. Treatment effects were summarised using random-effects meta-analysis and expressed as relative risk (RR) or mean difference (MD) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). The certainty of the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Fifteen studies involving 1,849 adult participants were included in the review. Twelve studies focused on patients with CKD (stages 1 to 5) who were not on dialysis, while three studies included patients undergoing haemodialysis. The potassium binders evaluated included calcium polystyrene sulfonate, sodium polystyrene sulfonate, patiromer, and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate. The studies varied in terms of drug administration routes, doses, and treatment durations, which ranged from 12 hours to 52 weeks (median duration: 4 weeks). Three of the studies employed a cross-over design. The mean age of participants ranged from 53.1 to 73 years. No studies were conducted in children. Several studies had methodological limitations, leading to low certainty in the results. Importantly, none of the studies were designed to evaluate the effects of treatment on cardiac arrhythmias or major gastrointestinal symptoms. Ten studies, involving 1,367 participants, compared potassium binders to placebo. The certainty of the evidence was low for all outcomes. Potassium binders were categorised into newer agents (patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate) and older agents (calcium polystyrene sulfonate and sodium polystyrene sulfonate). Patiromer and sodium zirconium cyclosilicate may have little or no effect on all-cause mortality (4 studies, 688 participants: RR 0.69, 95% CI 0.11 to 4.32; I² = 0%; low-certainty evidence) in patients with CKD. The effect of older potassium binders on all-cause mortality remains unknown. One cardiovascular death was reported in a study involving potassium binders, but no difference was observed between patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and placebo for cardiovascular mortality in CKD or haemodialysis patients. There was no evidence of a difference between patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate and placebo in terms of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) at the end of treatment (one study). Potassium binders had uncertain effects on nausea (3 studies, 229 participants: RR 2.10, 95% CI 0.65 to 6.78; I² = 0%; low-certainty evidence), diarrhoea (5 studies, 720 participants: RR 0.84, 95% CI 0.47 to 1.48; I² = 0%; low-certainty evidence), and vomiting (2 studies, 122 participants: RR 1.72, 95% CI 0.35 to 8.51; I² = 0%; low-certainty evidence) in CKD. Potassium binders may reduce serum potassium levels at the end of treatment (3 studies, 277 participants: MD -0.62 mEq/L, 95% CI -0.97 to -0.27; I² = 92%; low-certainty evidence) in CKD and haemodialysis patients. The effects of potassium binders on constipation were uncertain (4 studies, 425 participants: RR 1.58, 95% CI 0.71 to 3.52; I² = 0%; low-certainty evidence). Potassium binders may lower systolic blood pressure (2 studies, 369 participants: MD -3.73 mmHg, 95% CI -6.64 to -0.83; I² = 79%; low-certainty evidence) and diastolic blood pressure (one study) at the end of treatment. No studies reported data on cardiac arrhythmias or major gastrointestinal events. Calcium polystyrene sulfonate may have little or no effect on serum potassium levels at the end of treatment compared to sodium polystyrene sulfonate (2 studies, 117 participants: MD 0.38 mEq/L, 95% CI -0.03 to 0.79; I² = 42%; low-certainty evidence). There was no evidence of a difference in systolic blood pressure (one study), diastolic blood pressure (one study), or constipation (one study) between calcium polystyrene sulfonate and sodium polystyrene sulfonate. No differences were observed between high-dose and low-dose patiromer for outcomes such as sudden death, stroke, myocardial infarction, or constipation (one study). The comparative effects of administering potassium binders with or without food, laxatives, or sorbitol were highly uncertain due to insufficient data for meta-analysis. In conclusion, the evidence supporting clinical decision-making for the use of potassium binders in treating chronic hyperkalaemia in adults with CKD is of low certainty. No studies were identified in children. The available studies were not designed to assess the effects of treatment on clinically significant outcomes, such as cardiac arrhythmias or major gastrointestinal symptoms. This review highlights the need for a large, well-powered study comparing potassium binders to placebo, focusing on clinically relevant outcomes for patients, clinicians, and policymakers. Such data would also help evaluate the cost-effectiveness of these treatments, given the lack of definitive studies and the clinical importance of managing chronic hyperkalaemia in CKD patients.
